analysis.one_liner: Raises estate tax rates and lowers the tax-free threshold to $1 million, while closing common trust and valuation loopholes.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the House before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have restored a more aggressive estate tax: instead of the first $5 million of an inheritance being tax-free, only the first $1 million would be exempt, and rates would climb from 41% up to 55% on estates over $10 million, adjusted for inflation. It also would have closed several estate-planning techniques used to shrink taxable estates, including valuation discounts, short-term grantor retained annuity trusts (GRATs), and 'perpetual dynasty trusts,' which can currently carry wealth across generations largely untaxed. It also required executors to report the value of inherited assets so heirs cannot later claim a different, lower value for tax purposes.
analysis.who_benefits: The general public, as the beneficiary of federal revenue. Estates above $1 million — overwhelmingly held by the wealthiest households — would pay more tax. State governments would also regain a share through a restored federal credit for state inheritance taxes.

how_it_helps.text: Raises new estate tax rates from 41% (estates over $1 million) to 55% (estates over $10 million), replacing the current structure with a $5 million exemption [S2][S3].
Cuts the tax-free exclusion from $5 million to $1 million, with inflation adjustments after 2014, meaning far more large estates pay the tax [S2][S3].

Limits valuation discounts for family business interests and requires nonbusiness assets held in entities to be valued directly, closing techniques that shrink the taxable value of an estate [S2][S3].
Restricts short-term GRATs, which are designed so the taxable remainder is near zero, by requiring a minimum 10-year term and positive remainder value [S2][S3].
Ends the generation-skipping transfer exemption for perpetual dynasty trusts 90 years after they are created, so very large fortunes eventually face the tax [S2][S3].

Requires executors and gift-givers to report the value of each transferred interest to the Treasury and to recipients, and penalizes heirs who later claim a higher basis inconsistently with the estate return [S2][S3].
Restores the federal credit for state estate taxes paid, which expired after 2004, directing more revenue-sharing to state governments [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy families with estates above $1 million, who would face higher rates and a much lower exemption. Family businesses and farms in that range would face valuation rules that reduce discounts, and wealthy individuals using GRATs and dynasty trusts would lose planning tools. Estate-planning professionals would see reduced demand for the techniques the bill curtails.
analysis.who_pays_short: Estates over $1 million and their planners

drawbacks.text: A $1 million exemption is low enough that some moderately wealthy families, including owners of illiquid family farms or small businesses, would owe estate tax even without cash on hand; the bill's farm-friendly features are limited to valuation exceptions for working capital and actively operated real estate [S3].

Critics of the estate tax argue it taxes wealth that was already taxed when earned, and that compliance and valuation rules add administrative burdens for estates and executors; the bill adds new reporting and penalty provisions that increase filing requirements [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a tax base that falls almost entirely on the largest estates, and its anti-avoidance provisions would make the tax harder to sidestep. The main honest cost falls on a small set of wealthy families and on owners of illiquid family businesses caught by the $1 million threshold, though the bill includes some carve-outs for working farms and business assets. Overall, the burden is concentrated on households at the top of the wealth distribution, while the revenue would accrue broadly.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in February 2014, where it sat without a hearing or a vote, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott introduced the bill on February 14, 2014, with introductory remarks on February 11 [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on February 14, 2014, and no further action was taken on it [S5].
No representative signed on as a cosponsor during the bill's life [S4].
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and became void when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy estates above the current exemption threshold continue to benefit from the $5 million exemption and lower rates, and estate-planning practices the bill would have curtailed remain available. The public foregoes the additional revenue the bill would have raised.

for.name: Rep. Jim McDermott
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Sensible Estate Tax Act of 2014 and gave introductory remarks on the measure.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after receiving the referral.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority leadership controlling the House floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor, and with zero cosponsors there was no member pressure to schedule it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and the Republican-controlled House took no action on it.

industries.industry: Wealthy estates and family business owners
industries.note: Estates over $1 million would face rates from 41% to 55% and a much lower exemption, and owners of closely held businesses would lose valuation discounts. The cost falls on roughly the top fraction of one percent of decedents' estates, while the revenue would fund the federal budget broadly.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth management professionals
industries.note: The bill would curtail GRATs, valuation discounts, and perpetual dynasty trusts, the core techniques used to minimize estate tax bills. Their interest in keeping these tools runs against the public interest in collecting the tax as written.
